title: My Hero Academia Adventures
description:
🎭 248 Story Cards • Living World • 99% Canon Coverage
Version 1.0.5 — Corrected story cards, refined character appearances, and added missing canon elements.

You arrive at U.A. High School as Class 1-A’s newest transfer student, teacher or villain carrying a dangerous Quirk, a reputation you did not ask for, and the eyes of future heroes fixed on your back. Train, clash, bond, and survive in a cinematic My Hero Academia story where rivalries burn hot, friendships form under pressure, and every choice shapes how U.A. sees you.

Feedback / requests on discord appreciated : alexein9

Featuring Inner Self by @LewdLeah.

options.title: Class 1-A Student Intro
options.prompt:
You step through U.A. High School’s front gates with every camera pretending not to notice you.

The morning air is sharp, clean, almost too polished. Sunlight flashes across glass, steel, and white concrete, turning the campus into something halfway between a school and a fortress. The gates slide shut behind you with a low mechanical groan. Not loud. Just final.

You adjust the strap of your bag.

Student admitted in Class 1-A. The words sit on your shoulders heavier than the uniform.

At any other school, arriving late would mean whispers, awkward introductions, maybe a few curious stares from people who already had their friend groups sorted. At U.A., it means records reviewed by pro heroes. Quirk assessments. Combat footage. Notes from people who decided whether you were worth the risk before ever meeting you.

Class 1-A is somewhere ahead.

The class everyone talks about. The one with too much talent, too much trouble, and too many stories already attached to their names.

You cross the courtyard, feeling glances catch on you from every direction. Support Course students with tool cases. General Studies students pretending not to stare. Hero Course uniforms moving in clusters, voices lowering as you pass.

Someone already knows who you are. Someone probably thinks you do not belong here.

The main building rises in front of you, clean-lined and severe, its windows reflecting a version of you that looks calmer than you feel. Inside, a bell rings once, crisp and distant.

Your first day has already started.

And U.A. does not seem like the kind of place that waits for anyone.

The school year starts today.

options.title: Class 1-A Teacher Intro
options.prompt:
The staff entrance opens before you with a soft electronic chime.

No grand gates. No cheering students. No dramatic welcome from the symbol of hero education. Just polished floors, security glass, and a reception desk where your temporary faculty badge is scanned twice before anyone smiles.

U.A. High School is quieter from this side.

Not safer. Just quieter.

A staff member leads you through the administrative wing, past framed class photos, emergency maps, and doors marked with names that belong to pro heroes. Somewhere deeper in the building, students are already shouting, laughing, arguing, training, breaking rules, or pretending they are not about to.

You adjust your grip on your bag.

New teacher for Class 1-A. The words still feel strange.

At any other school, stepping into a classroom midyear would mean lesson plans, awkward introductions, and students testing how strict you are. At U.A., it means Quirk safety reports, combat permissions, medical histories, villain incident summaries, and a class roster that reads less like attendance and more like a disaster response file.

Aizawa’s notes are brief, blunt, and deeply unhelpful.

Nezu approved your placement personally.

That fact has not made anyone on staff look more relaxed.

You pass the teachers’ lounge and catch pieces of conversation that stop a little too quickly. Present Mic’s voice carries through one wall. Somewhere nearby, Power Loader is yelling about broken equipment. Recovery Girl gives you one sharp look from the infirmary doorway and immediately seems to know whether you slept enough.

Class 1-A is waiting ahead.

The class everyone talks about. Brilliant, reckless, loyal, traumatized, competitive, and far too used to adults arriving after the damage is already done.

The hallway outside their classroom is almost ordinary. Lockers. Sunlight. Scuffed floors. The low rumble of teenage voices behind the door.

Then something crashes inside.

A chair scrapes. Someone yells. Someone else laughs. Aizawa, standing beside the door in his sleeping bag, does not react.

He only looks at you and says, “Try not to make them worse.”

Your first class has already started.

And U.A. does not seem like the kind of place that gives teachers a warm-up day.

options.title: Villain Intro
options.prompt:
The first rule is simple: do not look like you are sneaking in.

People notice guilt faster than they notice lies.

So you walk toward U.A. High School with the same pace as everyone else. Not too fast. Not too slow. Bag at your side, shoulders loose, face arranged into something harmless. Around you, students flood the morning path in clean uniforms and loud little groups, arguing about homework, internships, lunch, training, hero rankings, ordinary things.

It would almost be funny, if the building ahead did not look so difficult to escape.

U.A. rises behind its gates in glass, steel, and white concrete, bright enough to make every shadow feel suspicious. Cameras watch from angles chosen by people who know where intruders look first. Security bots move with patient, ugly precision. Somewhere inside, pro heroes are drinking coffee, checking lesson plans, and pretending this school is not one of the most heavily guarded targets in Japan.

Your cover has held so far.

That is not the same as being safe.

At any other school, getting inside would be a matter of confidence, timing, and paperwork. Here, one curious teacher could ruin everything. One support student could notice a forged badge. One first-year with sharp instincts could look at you for half a second too long and turn an ordinary morning into a lockdown.

Class 1-A is somewhere inside.

That is the reason you are here.

Too much talent gathered in one room. Too many important names. Too many future heroes still young enough to be frightened, pressured, tricked, or broken before they understand what kind of story they are in.

You pass through the entrance checkpoint with your pulse steady and your expression bored. The scanner accepts the lie. The gate opens.

For one clean second, nobody stops you.

Inside the courtyard, U.A. feels painfully alive. Support Course students drag equipment across the path. General Studies students gossip near the steps. Hero Course uniforms move in bright clusters, loud and careless and dangerous.

Someone laughs nearby.

Someone glances at you.

You keep walking.

The main building waits ahead, clean-lined and severe, its windows reflecting a version of you that almost belongs here. Somewhere beyond those doors, a bell rings once.

Your first move has already started.

And U.A. has no idea what you came here to do.

cardPool.title: League of Villains Hideout
cardPool.value: {The League of Villains Hideout is an unstable villain gathering place, often disguised as a grimy bar, abandoned room, or hidden safehouse. It feels cramped, smoky, underfunded, and watched from every angle. Casual conversation can become a threat without warning because everyone carries trauma, ambition, and suspicion. Loyalty is real but jagged. Scene Hooks: Shigaraki scratching while planning violence, Kurogiri maintaining order, Twice spiraling into jokes and panic, Dabi needling someone, Toga getting too interested, informants arriving, police pressure, and All For One’s influence hanging over the room.}

cardPool.value: {The U.A. Support Course Lab is a noisy, cluttered workshop full of half-built costumes, test rigs, tools, smoke stains, spare parts, safety posters everyone ignores, and machines that probably should not be humming. Support students and staff build, repair, and test hero costumes, mobility gear, capture tools, sensors, and Quirk-specific equipment. Scene Hooks: costume upgrades, dangerous prototypes, accidental explosions, rushed repairs before exams, Power Loader scolding everyone, Mei-style sales pitches, and heroes learning that better gear cannot replace better judgment.}

cardPool.title: Ground Gamma
cardPool.value: {Ground Gamma is U.A.'s sprawling industrial training ground, a maze of pipes, tanks, walkways and factory-like structures. Dense obstacles create blind spots, vertical routes and opportunities for ambushes, scouting and coordinated capture. Class 1-A and Class 1-B use it for their joint team battles. Large attacks can collapse cover or endanger teammates; mobility, communication and knowledge of the terrain matter as much as raw force.}

cardPool.title: Hero Billboard Chart
cardPool.value: {The Hero Billboard Chart ranks Pro Heroes based on achievements, public approval, incident resolution, social contribution, and overall impact. Rankings shape fame, funding, agency recruitment, media attention, sponsorships, and public trust, but they can also distort hero priorities. Some heroes chase rank as proof of worth, while others resent being judged like celebrities. Billboard scenes should involve ceremonies, interviews, agency pressure, scandals, fan reactions, rival rankings, and the conflict between visible heroism and quiet service. The Chart is useful for showing how hero society turns protection into performance, competition, and political capital.}

cardPool.title: Provisional License Exam
cardPool.value: {The Provisional License Exam tests whether hero students can be trusted to use their Quirks in public under limited legal authority. It evaluates combat judgment, rescue priorities, teamwork, communication, civilian handling, restraint, and the ability to adapt against unfamiliar students from rival schools. Exam scenes should feel crowded, tactical, and stressful: target zones, rival teams, rescue simulations, fake civilians, disqualifications, instructors watching for recklessness, and students realizing that power alone does not earn permission to act. The exam is useful for rivalries, forced alliances, public failure, clever tactics, and lessons about professionalism under pressure.}

cardPool.title: Forest Training Camp
cardPool.value: {Forest Training Camp is an off-campus intensive training environment where hero students are pushed through wilderness drills, Quirk conditioning, survival exercises, teamwork tests, and limited-comfort living away from normal school structure. The setting is ideal for exhaustion, rivalry, camp meals, night patrols, mentor pressure, and sudden danger in isolated terrain. Training Camp scenes should emphasize muddy trails, dark woods, separated groups, stamina limits, teacher ambush drills, shared cabins, fear after sunset, and the way remote environments make both bonding and crisis sharper. It works for slice-of-life growth, horror tension, or villain attacks far from easy backup.}

cardPool.title: U.A. Sports Festival
cardPool.value: {The U.A. Sports Festival is a televised annual competition, with separate events for each school year. Hero, General Studies, Support and Management students can participate; General Studies students may attract Hero Course attention, while Support students advertise inventions. The first-year events include an obstacle race, cavalry battle and individual tournament. Pro agencies scout candidates for internships. Public victories, embarrassing defeats and family pressure make it a major test of confidence as well as tactics.}

cardPool.title: Kamino Ward
cardPool.value: {Kamino Ward is an urban district suited for high-stakes villain operations, warehouses, hidden facilities, residential blocks, and public disasters that unfold under media attention. It carries the feeling of a city space where secret criminal infrastructure can suddenly erupt into national crisis. Kamino scenes should involve surveillance, rescue pressure, hostage risk, collapsing buildings, public fear, and the terrifying visibility of hero failure or success. Use Kamino for hideout raids, villain transport, media helicopters, desperate evacuations, and confrontations where the outcome affects public faith in heroes. The location should feel ordinary until the scale of hidden danger becomes impossible to deny.}

cardPool.title: Hosu City
cardPool.value: {Hosu City is a dense urban district known for alleys, elevated roads, train lines, commercial zones, and the kind of crowded infrastructure where hero patrols, villain attacks, and civilian panic can escalate fast. It is useful for stories involving street-level hero work, emergency response, ideological violence, and students encountering the consequences of real patrols. Hosu scenes should emphasize narrow sightlines, fleeing civilians, sirens, smoke, separated teams, rooftops, blocked roads, and the difference between school exercises and uncontrolled public danger. It works especially well for vigilante themes, hero-killer rumors, and moral pressure around revenge versus rescue.}

cardPool.title: Musutafu City
cardPool.value: {Musutafu City is the urban area associated with U.A. High School, mixing ordinary neighborhoods, commercial streets, train routes, hero offices, schools, alleys, and disaster-prone public spaces. It works as the default everyday city backdrop for students and heroes: convenience stores after training, patrol routes, crowds recognizing uniforms, villains hiding in normal streets, and civilians expecting heroes to appear quickly. Musutafu scenes should balance normal life with sudden danger, showing how hero society makes the extraordinary feel routine. Use it for slice-of-life outings, urban patrols, internships, villain sightings, media encounters, and the awkward overlap between school life and public hero expectations.}

cardPool.title: Police Force
cardPool.value: {The Police Force handles criminal investigation, arrests, evidence, public safety coordination, and legal procedure in a society where licensed heroes perform much of the public-facing combat. Police often work beside heroes but do not have the same social glamour, creating a practical divide between investigation and spectacle. Police scenes should involve reports, warrants, questioning, crime scenes, chain of custody, surveillance footage, civilian witnesses, and frustration when heroes act faster than paperwork allows. Good police characters should ground the story in procedure and consequences: evidence matters, arrests must hold up legally, and even heroic instincts can ruin a case if handled recklessly.}

cardPool.title: Tartarus Prison

Cameras and sensors monitor dangerous inmates continuously; automated guns respond to threatening movements or signs of Quirk activation. Restraints and armed surveillance maintain containment, not a universal Quirk-canceling field. Restricted visits, interrogations, contested treatment of prisoners and breaches of its layered security create high-stakes encounters.}

cardPool.title: High-End Nomu
cardPool.value: {High-End Nomu are advanced Nomu with stronger bodies, multiple coordinated Quirks, greater intelligence, and enough personality fragments to speak, strategize, or choose targets. Unlike basic Nomu, High-Ends can feel like monstrous specialists rather than mindless weapons, often combining regeneration, mobility, raw power, and tactical instincts. They should unsettle heroes because they blur the line between villain, corpse, weapon, and person. High-End scenes work best for escalation: brutal surprise attacks, impossible regeneration, tactical adaptation, civilian panic, and experienced Pro Heroes being forced past safe limits. Even victory should feel costly, messy, and medically disturbing.}

cardPool.title: Nomu
cardPool.value: {Nomu are artificial Quirk-modified beings created through unethical experimentation, body alteration, and multiple-Quirk implantation. Most lack normal speech, identity, or independent will, acting as weapons directed by handlers or programmed instincts. Their abilities vary from simple brute strength to regeneration, flight, shock absorption, sensory tracking, and specialized combat traits. Nomu scenes should feel unnatural and frightening: delayed pain response, distorted bodies, sudden adaptation, animalistic obedience, and heroes realizing they are fighting someone who may once have been human. Nomu work best as horror-combat threats, evidence of hidden laboratories, or moral pressure around what villains are willing to create.}

cardPool.title: Deika City
cardPool.value: {Deika City is an ordinary-looking urban center that can hide deep Meta Liberation Army influence beneath civic normality. Its streets, offices, homes, and public spaces may seem peaceful until coordinated residents, businesses, and officials reveal shared ideology or prepared combat roles. Deika works best as a paranoia-heavy location: too-clean neighborhoods, smiling civilians with secret loyalties, hidden weapons, sudden mass mobilization, propaganda posters, corporate fronts, and heroes realizing the battlefield is not a hideout but an entire community. Scenes here should emphasize scale, surveillance, ambush, and the horror of a city turning against outsiders at once.}

cardPool.title: Detnerat Company
cardPool.value: {Detnerat Company is a major support-item and lifestyle corporation secretly tied to Quirk liberation ideology. Publicly, it sells products designed to help people live with their Quirks; privately, its money, technology, logistics, and executive network can support militant organizing. Detnerat works well as a bridge between corporate respectability and hidden extremism: clean offices above weapons testing, polite executives funding radicals, support gear with ideological branding, and employees who may not know where the money flows. Detnerat scenes should mix product demos, corporate pressure, suspicious shipments, secret labs, and the uneasy question of when accommodation becomes militarization.}

cardPool.title: Paranormal Liberation Front
cardPool.value: {The Paranormal Liberation Front is a massive villain coalition formed from organized liberation ideology, criminal power, and anti-hero-society resentment. It combines militant hierarchy, propaganda, corporate resources, underground fighters, and charismatic figureheads into a force large enough to threaten national stability. Unlike small villain gangs, the PLF can mobilize cells, command cities, manipulate media, and pressure society through both violence and ideology. PLF scenes should involve scale: coordinated uprisings, coded orders, political speeches, hidden bases, divided commanders, uneasy alliances, and the fear that ordinary civilians may secretly support the collapse of hero regulation.}

cardPool.title: Meta Liberation Army
cardPool.value: {The Meta Liberation Army is an ideological militant organization built around Quirk liberation: the belief that people should freely use their abilities without government restriction. Publicly hidden behind companies, politics, media, and civic influence, the MLA frames Quirk regulation as oppression and personal ability as natural freedom. Its members range from true believers to opportunists, soldiers, executives, and civilians radicalized by resentment. MLA scenes should feel organized, ideological, and unsettlingly normal: corporate meetings hiding insurgency, public speeches, propaganda, citywide coordination, liberation rhetoric, mass combat, and moral pressure around whether Quirk law protects society or cages it.}

cardPool.title: U.A. High School

Its facilities include specialized training grounds, advanced security, dorms, medical support, workshops, and disaster simulations. U.A. is prestigious but intense: students are pushed toward professional standards early, often facing public scrutiny, rivalry, danger, and moral pressure. Teachers are usually active or former Pro Heroes, so lessons tend to be practical, harsh, and survival-focused. U.A. represents opportunity, pressure, ambition, and the uneasy belief that teenagers can be shaped into symbols of public trust.}

cardPool.title: Vigilantes
cardPool.value: {Vigilantes are unlicensed individuals who use their Quirks or skills to fight crime, protect civilians, or pursue justice without legal authorization. Some act where heroes are absent, corrupt, too slow, or bound by procedure; others are reckless, vengeful, or addicted to the feeling of power. Hero law treats vigilantes as criminals regardless of intent, creating tension with police, Pro Heroes, and civilians who may secretly approve of them. Vigilante scenes should sit in a moral gray zone: alley rescues, hidden injuries, anonymous tips, illegal patrols, pursuit by heroes, and hard choices where doing the right thing may still break the law.}

cardPool.title: Villains
cardPool.value: {Villains are people or groups who use Quirks, resources, influence, or violence to exploit, disrupt, or reject hero society. Their motives vary: greed, trauma, ideology, revenge, survival, coercion, alienation, or the desire to prove society hypocritical. Some are organized criminals, some are radicals, some are broken people lashing out, and some are predators who enjoy power. Villains should not all feel the same; each should have a method, pressure point, and reason they act outside the law. Scenes with villains work best when danger reflects personality: manipulation, hostage pressure, ambushes, moral dilemmas, public fear, or personal grudges.}

cardPool.title: Hero Students
cardPool.value: {Hero Students are trainees enrolled in licensed hero programs such as U.A.’s Hero Course. They study academics, combat, rescue, teamwork, ethics, public conduct, Quirk control, and crisis judgment while still being minors with ordinary fears and rivalries. They may use Quirks under school supervision and can gain field experience through approved exercises, internships, and licensing paths. Hero Students live between two pressures: society expects them to become reliable protectors, while their teachers know mistakes can maim or kill. Scenes with Hero Students should mix teenage awkwardness, ambition, competition, exhaustion, friendship, and the weight of growing up under public expectations.}

cardPool.title: Quirk Counseling Centers
cardPool.value: {Quirk Counseling Centers are institutions meant to help children understand, regulate, and socially adapt to their Quirks as they grow. In theory, they provide emotional support, safety education, family guidance, and healthy identity formation. In practice, quality varies widely: some counselors help children thrive, while others push conformity, suppress uncomfortable traits, or fail those with frightening, stigmatized, or socially inconvenient Quirks. Scenes involving Quirk Counseling should focus on childhood pressure, family fear, institutional blind spots, shame, coping tools, misdiagnosis, and the difference between teaching control and teaching someone to hate part of themselves.}

cardPool.title: Shiketsu High School
cardPool.value: {Shiketsu High School is an elite hero-training academy known for discipline, formal conduct, strict uniforms, and institutional pride. Often treated as U.A.’s rival, Shiketsu emphasizes order, composure, obedience, and the idea that heroes must project authority as well as power. Its students are usually polished, serious, and tightly trained, though individual personalities can clash beneath the uniformity. Shiketsu scenes should highlight rivalry, culture shock, strict etiquette, competitive exams, joint training, ideological disagreements with U.A., and the tension between personal emotion and the school’s demand for heroic professionalism.}

cardPool.title: U.S.J. (Unforeseen Simulation Joint)
cardPool.value: {U.S.J., the Unforeseen Simulation Joint, is U.A. High School’s massive indoor disaster-training facility. It contains multiple simulated emergency zones such as flood, fire, landslide, storm, mountain, ruin, and urban-collapse environments. The facility teaches rescue prioritization, hazard awareness, civilian evacuation, and adapting when conditions change faster than plans. U.S.J. scenes should feel chaotic and practical: broken visibility, separated teams, injured civilians or dummies, environmental dangers, time pressure, teacher instructions, and the reminder that hero work is not only about defeating villains but keeping frightened people alive.}

cardPool.title: Ground Beta
cardPool.value: {Ground Beta is one of U.A. High School’s large outdoor combat-training zones, built to simulate dense urban streets, industrial structures, alleys, rooftops, and destructible obstacles. It is ideal for pursuit drills, rescue routes, team battles, villain simulations, capture exercises, and collateral-damage lessons. The environment rewards mobility, scouting, vertical movement, ambush awareness, and controlled force. Ground Beta scenes should emphasize positioning, sightlines, civilians represented by dummies or actors, property damage, unstable terrain, teacher surveillance, and students learning that winning a fight means little if the city around them is ruined.}

cardPool.title: U.A. Cafeteria
cardPool.value: {U.A. Cafeteria is the school’s main dining hall, operated by Lunch Rush and designed to feed students, staff, and visiting heroes after intense academic and physical training. Meals are high-calorie, balanced, and fast, turning the cafeteria into both a recovery station and social hub. It is where rivalries simmer over lunch trays, exhausted students decompress, rumors spread, teachers observe morale, and friendships form through ordinary routine. Cafeteria scenes should mix food, noise, teasing, fatigue, seating politics, nutrition after Quirk strain, and small emotional reveals that feel safer because everyone is pretending it is just lunch.}

cardPool.title: Heights Alliance
cardPool.value: {Heights Alliance is U.A. High School’s fortified student dormitory complex, built to keep Hero Course students close to campus, teachers, medical care, and emergency response systems. It provides private rooms, shared lounges, kitchens, training access, and constant peer contact. The dorms are safer than ordinary housing but emotionally intense: classmates see each other tired, injured, homesick, jealous, awkward, and unguarded. Heights Alliance scenes work best for slice-of-life tension, late-night conversations, rivalries softening, group meals, pranks, recovery after battles, teacher check-ins, and sudden alarms that turn domestic calm into hero readiness.}

cardPool.title: The Big Three
cardPool.value: {The Big Three are U.A. High School’s top senior Hero Course students: Mirio Togata, Tamaki Amajiki, and Nejire Hado. They represent different forms of excellence: Mirio’s fearless mastery and charisma, Tamaki’s anxious but terrifying versatility, and Nejire’s energetic aerial power and curiosity. To younger students, they can feel inspiring, intimidating, or impossible to catch up to. Big Three scenes should showcase mentorship, demonstrations, sparring, rescue drills, emotional contrast, and the gap between raw talent and refined experience. Their group dynamic balances Mirio’s sunshine, Tamaki’s dread, and Nejire’s sparkling chaos.}

cardPool.title: Internships
cardPool.value: {Hero Internships place hero students under active Pro Heroes or agencies for real-world training, supervised patrols, rescue exposure, combat observation, and professional evaluation. Internships accelerate growth but also expose students to danger, bureaucracy, public scrutiny, and ethical problems that classrooms can only simulate. Good mentors teach restraint, communication, and judgment; bad placements may treat students as publicity, labor, or liabilities. Internship scenes should involve patrol routines, sudden emergencies, mentor tests, agency politics, awkward professionalism, student insecurity, and moments where training collides with the frightening unpredictability of real hero work.}

cardPool.title: Hero Agencies
cardPool.value: {Hero Agencies are professional organizations run by licensed heroes, functioning as emergency-response teams, patrol offices, training sites, public relations machines, and businesses. Agencies vary widely: some are elite combat units, some specialize in rescue or investigation, and some lean heavily into branding and sponsorships. They employ sidekicks, interns, analysts, drivers, support staff, and media handlers. Agency scenes should mix professional hero work with workplace pressure: patrol briefings, paperwork, rankings competition, sponsorship concerns, intern evaluations, civilian complaints, emergency dispatches, and the contrast between heroic ideals and the daily grind of public service.}

cardPool.title: Hero Public Safety Commission
cardPool.value: {The Hero Public Safety Commission is the government body overseeing hero licensing, rankings, public order, investigations, and covert operations. It presents itself as the guardian of stability, but its priorities often favor control, optics, and national security over transparency or personal freedom. The Commission can support heroes with resources, intelligence, and authority, yet also pressure them into secrecy, obedience, or morally gray missions. Scenes involving the Commission should feel procedural, tense, and political: closed-door briefings, suppressed evidence, rankings pressure, classified assignments, media management, and conflicts between individual conscience and institutional stability.}

cardPool.title: The League of Villains
cardPool.value: {The League of Villains is led by Tomura Shigaraki, initially backed by All For One and Kurogiri. Its core includes Dabi, Toga, Twice, Spinner and Mr. Compress; its wider membership changes through recruitment, arrests and deaths. Members have conflicting ambitions but find belonging among outcasts. Shigaraki targets faith in heroes, while Giran brokers recruits and supplies. Raids, hideouts, scarce resources and loyalty under pressure define its operations; it later merges with the Meta Liberation Army to form the Paranormal Liberation Front.}

cardPool.title: Hero Licenses
cardPool.value: {Hero Licenses are legal certifications allowing controlled public Quirk use for rescue, defense, patrol, and villain response. Full licenses grant professional authority; provisional licenses give students limited permission under defined conditions. Licensing creates accountability but also friction: a person may have the power to help before they have permission to act. Heroes and students must consider evidence, civilians, property damage, chain of command, and whether Quirk use is legally justified. License-related scenes work well for exams, patrol restrictions, moral dilemmas, disciplinary hearings, emergency exceptions, and conflicts between immediate rescue instincts and official procedure.}

cardPool.title: Quirks
cardPool.value: {Quirks are heritable superhuman traits found in roughly 80% of humanity, usually manifesting by age four, sometimes at birth. The three broad types are Emitter, Transformation and Mutant/Heteromorph; individual abilities can share characteristics. A Quirk factor includes the biological mechanisms enabling the power. Training improves control, output and stamina but does not erase activation conditions or bodily limits. Mutation, inheritance and social prejudice shape identity. Public and professional use is regulated; a powerful Quirk is not itself a hero license.}

Chisaki plans to sell both the bullets and a remedy, making heroes and villains dependent on the Hassaikai. Its base hides tunnels, laboratories and captives beneath a conventional residence.}

cardPool.value: {The Shie Hassaikai manufactures Quirk-destroying ammunition using material harvested from Eri's body and her Rewind power. Early versions temporarily disable Quirks; completed rounds destroy the target's Quirk factor and cause lasting loss. They do not copy or transfer a Quirk. Chisaki's scheme pairs sales of the weapon with a restorative product to control both sides of the market. Mirio loses Permeation protecting Eri from a completed round; her later trained Rewind restores it. Supply is scarce and tied to exploitation, theft and laboratory research.}

cardPool.title: Trigger
cardPool.value: {Trigger is a drug that temporarily amplifies a user's existing Quirk, often at the cost of judgment and bodily control. Potency and duration differ between formulations; some incidents produce severe transformations or violent rampages. It does not grant a random new Quirk. In Naruhata, the Villain Factory uses doses and engineered attacks to gather data, with Queen Bee secretly injecting victims. Other criminals use it to push powers beyond normal limits, including Mimic's building-scale control. Investigations involve victims as well as willing users and dealers.}

cardPool.title: Quirk Singularity
cardPool.value: {Quirk Singularity is the theory that increasingly powerful and complex Quirks will eventually outpace human bodies and the ability to control them. Dr. Garaki advocates the theory; unusually strong abilities among young children illustrate its concern. It is a prediction, not proof that every Quirk user must become violent or that catastrophe is inevitable. Humarise distorts it into an extermination ideology. Research, ethical disputes, dangerous childhood manifestations and efforts to support overwhelmed users offer recurring conflicts.}

cardPool.title: Quirk Awakening
cardPool.value: {A Quirk awakening is an exceptional expansion of an existing ability, often emerging under extreme emotional or physical pressure. It differs from ordinary training, newly learned techniques or simply discovering a previously misunderstood function. Toga gains access to the Quirks of people she transforms into when her feelings meet the necessary condition; Shigaraki's Decay develops vastly greater spread. An awakening remains connected to the original power and can have costs. Stress does not guarantee one or justify unrelated new abilities.}

cardPool.title: Naruhata
cardPool.value: {Naruhata is the Tokyo neighborhood at the center of Vigilantes. Shopping streets, apartment blocks, rooftops and small venues connect its residents more closely than hero rankings do. Koichi's modest home becomes an informal meeting place for Pop☆Step, Knuckleduster and their acquaintances. Street performances and everyday errands coexist with Trigger incidents, illegal rescues and police investigations. Local witnesses, shopkeepers and former delinquents can offer practical help; public use of a Quirk can still bring legal trouble even when the intention is rescue.}

cardPool.title: Villain Factory
cardPool.value: {The Villain Factory is All For One's covert operation in Vigilantes, using Trigger, human experimentation and engineered attacks to develop weapons and gather combat data. Queen Bee creates incidents through unsuspecting hosts and drugged victims; Number 6 is an advanced artificial operative with Overclock and additional modifications. Anonymous handlers and disposable attackers conceal the leadership. Its work connects neighborhood violence to the later Nomu program. Victims may be coerced, possessed or altered, making capture and rescue more complicated than defeating a willing criminal.}

cardPool.title: Wild Wild Pussycats
cardPool.value: {The Wild Wild Pussycats are a four-person rescue team: Mandalay coordinates through Telepath, Pixie-Bob shapes terrain with Earth Flow, Tiger handles close combat with Pliabody, and Ragdoll locates people through Search before All For One steals it. Ragdoll continues supporting the team afterward. Their cat costumes and theatrical greetings conceal demanding professional standards. Mountain rescue and U.A.'s forest training camp suit their combined skills. They care for Kota and protect students fiercely, balancing playful teasing with punishing practical drills.}

cardPool.title: Ketsubutsu Academy High School
cardPool.value: {Ketsubutsu Academy High School trains aspiring heroes and competes with U.A. Emi Fukukado, Ms. Joke, teaches the group including Yo Shindo, Tatami Nakagame, Shikkui Makabe and Itejiro Toteki. At the Provisional License Exam these students are second-years, older than U.A.'s first-year entrants. Friendly introductions can conceal carefully planned competitive tactics. School rivalry, joint exercises, licensing exams and evacuation patrols provide meetings beyond U.A.; Ms. Joke's teasing familiarity with Aizawa complicates the formal atmosphere.}

cardPool.title: Humarise
cardPool.value: {Humarise is Flect Turn's extremist organization in World Heroes' Mission. It treats Quirks as a curse and misuses Quirk Singularity theory to justify killing Quirk users. Its international cells include Quirk-bearing agents such as Beros, whose devotion is framed as atonement. Trigger Bombs release a substance that drives Quirks catastrophically out of control; the organization threatens coordinated attacks across countries. Secret facilities, compromised authorities, missing researchers and stolen bomb-disarming information draw heroes into its conspiracy.}

cardPool.title: I-Island
cardPool.value: {I-Island is a mobile artificial island devoted to Quirk research and support technology. Scientists, engineers and families live alongside tightly secured laboratories; I-Expo brings visiting heroes and guests to see new inventions. David and Melissa Shield work here. Unlike ordinary Japanese streets, the island permits public Quirk use, but its advanced security can restrict movement and become a danger if hijacked. Research tours, prototype demonstrations, corporate secrecy and disputes over dangerous inventions create encounters beyond conventional hero combat.}

cardPool.title: Support Equipment
cardPool.value: {Support equipment helps a user apply an existing Quirk or compensate for its limits through engineering. Examples include Bakugo's sweat-storage gauntlets, Jiro's amplifiers, Aizawa's capture cloth and Shinso's Persona Chords voice changer. Some tools work for Quirkless users too. U.A.'s Support Course, overseen by Power Loader, develops and tests designs; Mei Hatsume eagerly recruits testers. Gear requires fitting, maintenance and practice and can break or run out of resources. An item does not automatically reproduce another person's Quirk or remove the user's physical limits.}
